Lessons.Title: Fractions Round Table PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: First Edition 2021 Grade 3 Unit 8 Lesson 3 is an open mathematical dialogue about the meaning and comparison of fractions, including how whole numbers relate to fractions. The teacher HTML and its locally cached preparation page were reviewed. Its eight original table claims are present in the saved HTML, but the two original activity-image pixels and a standalone student PDF were not independently examined. First-party descriptions here are NOT copies of the two images.

Warm-up: What Do You Know About 1/8? (10 minutes). Ask students to describe one of eight equal-size parts of a whole, display a partitioned interval or area, and explain why changing the whole changes the length of the part. Invite more than one valid verbal and visual model, not one fixed numerical answer.

Activity 1: Fractions Round Table (35 minutes), groups of FOUR. Groups discuss eight thematic source claims covering whether fractions must be less than 1, fractions on the number line, numerator and denominator meanings, whole numbers as fractions, fractions as whole numbers, comparisons of 1/2 with 1/3, and lengths measured as fractions. The original visible public HTML embeds two source images with the table, and the teacher must inspect their exact layout. Do not assume every group is required to complete all eight statements; the teacher may prioritize a subset.

This is a THREE-ROUND discussion for EACH statement attempted, not a three-question multiple-choice quiz. Round 1: everyone chooses agree, disagree or unsure and justifies an initial belief. Round 2: discuss another member position, again agree/disagree/unsure and allow opinions to change. Round 3: independently circle a final choice after hearing reasons and explain any revisions. Student participation, mathematical evidence and changes of mind need teacher review.

Source claim A: the idea that ALL fractions are smaller than 1 is false; examples 5/4 and 3/2 represent values above 1. Source claim B: fractions do locate on number lines with uniform units and suitable partitions. Claim C: the numerator does not by itself decide how big one equal part is; numerator counts parts taken. Claim D: denominator identifies the number of equal-sized pieces in one whole under the usual fraction interpretation.

Source claim E: whole numbers can all be expressed as fractions, for instance 3 = 3/1. Claim F: it does NOT follow that all fractions are whole numbers, since 1/8 is not, while 6/2 is. Claim G: 1/2 exceeds 1/3 when the SAME whole is being partitioned; the assertion is not automatically valid for portions of DIFFERENT size wholes. Claim H: fractions describe lengths, such as 1/8 of a unit-length interval.

Teacher synthesis (about 10 minutes): invite students to describe which statement generated disagreement and what evidence caused them to reconsider. Accept an initial unsure response, oral representations and revision when reasoned. Particularly distinguish fraction quantity from the magnitude of the chosen whole in comparisons.

The original Round Table Reflection Cool-down (5 minutes) is publisher-gated and not copied or scored in Edulytics. An independent Edulytics self-check may be offered but cannot replace the source discussion or teacher assessment. Source attribution retained; no publisher graphics embedded; .NET tests written, compilation/Stage D/academic approval not claimed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parts of the same whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: Numerator indicates how many equal-size parts; denominator how many such parts compose the whole.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Only compare fractions as physical portions using the same reference whole.
KeyConcepts.Example: For the same whole, 1/2 > 1/3; for different wholes, physical length comparison needs scale.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fractions and whole numbers
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fractions represent rational quantities including some whole numbers and values exceeding one.
KeyConcepts.Rule: n=n/1 and 6/2=3 but 1/8 is not an integer.

KeyConcepts.Title: Revision after discussion
KeyConcepts.Definition: A three-round discussion records individual starting position, peer exchange and final position.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Evidence and justification, not answer-only selection, determine readiness.
KeyConcepts.Example: Student first agrees every fraction is less than 1; then sees 5/4 > 1 and explains a change of mind.

WorkedExamples.Title: Counterexample to always less than 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Are all fractions below one?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show a fraction whose numerator exceeds the denominator.
Steps: Represent 5/4 as five equal quarter units.
Four quarters make one whole, with one quarter remaining.
5/4 is greater than one; the universal claim is false.
WorkedExamples.Check: A single valid counterexample disproves an ALL claim.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reason about a conditional comparison
WorkedExamples.Question: Is half always longer than a third?
WorkedExamples.Method: Check the referent whole before comparing physical lengths.
Steps: For a small whole of length 2: its half is length 1.
For a larger whole of length 6: its third is length 2.
The lengths differ according to the original wholes.
WorkedExamples.Answer: On the same whole, half exceeds third; across different wholes physical portion lengths cannot be compared by labels alone.
WorkedExamples.Check: Separate abstract fractions on a common unit number line from measurements of different wholes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mark every fraction as a number less than one.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Fractions such as 5/4 and 3/1 reach or exceed one.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use model counterexamples, including whole-number fractions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat numerator as size of each equal part.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: For a given whole, the denominator determines the equal division size.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State that denominator partitions the whole and numerator counts selected equal pieces.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original source uses agree/disagree/unsure across three rounds and values mathematical discourse.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep initial, peer-response and final reasoning; allow justified changes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Grade the eight discussion claims as isolated scalar answers.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Group debate, context and verbal justification are source requirements.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Apply teacher rubric; do not coerce answers into auto-graded numeric response.

SummaryPoints: Activity: groups of 4, 35 minutes, debate source statement cards in 3 rounds.
Eight source claim themes: bounds, number line, numerator/denominator, whole numbers, 1/2 vs 1/3 and length.
Agree, disagree and unsure are permitted at each stage; student may revise.
Review source image statements and oral rationale with teacher; original PDF and images not independently inspected; publisher Cool-down not copied.
